schools.summary: Gill supposes a consultation in which the three friends settled a plan and the order of proceeding, takes Eliphaz for the senior of them, and notes that he said nothing by way of condolence but reproached Job as wicked and hypocritical.

Henry credits the opening with real modesty and tenderness, grants that the charge of faint-heartedness had too much ground, calls the charge of hypocrisy utterly groundless, and catches Eliphaz using Satan's own word when he says only that the trouble touches Job.

Clarke has the friends awed into seven days' silence until Eliphaz loses the feeling of the friend in the haughtiness of the censor, yet judges the beginning plausible and far from insincere; Wesley reads the closing verse as the plain charge that Job's religion was mere talk and appearance.

Ellicott finds a conspicuous want of feeling in Eliphaz, thinks he almost rejoices that one who helped so many now needs help himself, and states the premise governing all the friends' speeches, that it is the wicked who suffer and all who suffer must be wicked.

debates.issue: What moved Eliphaz to speak as he does

positions.view: Clarke calls the opening plausible and certainly far from insincere, since it is a duty to rise up on God's part even at the cost of grieving a friend.
Ellicott finds a conspicuous want of feeling, with the outward signs of sympathy given but an almost malevolent satisfaction underneath.

outliers.view: That the note struck here, that the wicked suffer and all who suffer must be wicked, is in one form or another the sum and substance of everything the three friends have to say.

themes: the seven days' silence broken
wilt thou be grieved if we speak
thou hast instructed many
it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled
is not this thy fear, thy confidence
1.pericope_label: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered: thou hast instructed many, but now it is come upon thee

schools.summary: Gill sifts what innocence and perishing can mean here and lays out three readings of the lions, by God himself, by beasts of prey, or by oppressive rulers, preferring the last.

Henry distinguishes final from temporal perishing, refutes the principle with Abel and Lot, and suspects that in tracing destruction to a blast and a breath Eliphaz points at the wind that blew the house down on Job's children.

Clarke gathers the parallels for ploughing iniquity and reaping the same, lists the derivations of the five words for lion and then deflates his own list; Wesley takes the opening question as the bare charge that Job is guilty of a secret crime now found out.

Ellicott calls the question a half-truth that is after all true, offers the more gracious reading of Eliphaz's object, and infers from the five words for lion that such animals were common and various in Job's country.

debates.issue: What the question about the innocent perishing is worth

positions.view: Wesley takes it as an accusation: Job is guilty of some secret crime which has now found him out.
Ellicott thinks the more probable and more gracious object is to show Job that if he is what he was taken to be, that is itself a ground of hope.
Henry denies the principle outright for temporal calamity, since Abel was innocent and cut off early and Lot was burnt out of house and harbour.

debates.issue: Who the lions of the closing verses are

positions.view: Gill reports that one Jewish commentator took them for God himself and two others for actual beasts of prey, but prefers oppressive rulers, and the other voices agree.

outliers.view: That Eliphaz, in tracing the destruction of the wicked to the blast and breath of God, may be pointing at the wind that blew the house down on Job's children, as though they were sinners above all men.

themes: who ever perished, being innocent
they that plough iniquity reap the same
the blast of God
the five names for the lion
whether Job is the lion meant
7.pericope_label: Who ever perished, being innocent: the old lion perisheth for lack of prey

schools.summary: Gill reports that some have called the vision a fiction and some a diabolical one, and answers on three grounds: nothing in its manner or matter disagrees with a divine vision, Eliphaz was a good man, and Job never charges him with falsehood here.

Henry holds the apparition real and not a fancy, will not let false visions disprove apparitions altogether, and judges that the vision grounds a reproof of Job's murmuring but not a charge of hypocrisy.

Clarke grants the vision but suspects that Eliphaz professes it to give himself the more authority and applies it otherwise than it was designed, and quotes a writer who finds no rival to the passage in ancient or modern poetry; Wesley distinguishes dreams, given to men asleep, from visions, given to men awake.

Ellicott notes that the word was literally stolen for him, that the term for little occurs only once more and in Job's own mouth, and denies that spiritual essences can be seen by the bodily eye, allowing instead that inner perceptions may be vivid enough to seem outward.

debates.issue: What it was that passed before Eliphaz's face

positions.view: Henry holds it a real apparition, an image plainly before his eyes, and defends the possibility of apparitions of spirits.
Wesley takes it for an angel in visible shape, since otherwise it could not have been discerned.
Gill reports a reading that makes it a stormy wind, but prefers an angel in human form.
Ellicott calls the notion of seeing a spirit absurd in itself, and substitutes an inner perception so vivid as to take on the character of an outward manifestation.

outliers.view: That Eliphaz professes the vision in order to give himself the more authority, and applied it in a different way from what the communication itself designed.

themes: a thing secretly brought to me
visions of the night
fear came upon me, and trembling
a spirit passed before my face
whether the vision was genuine
12.pericope_label: A spirit passed before my face: the hair of my flesh stood up

schools.summary: Gill objects that no revelation was needed to teach what reason already shows, so that the comparative sense cannot be the point of the oracle, and holds that the oracle itself runs to the end of the chapter.

Henry takes the question as a reproof of murmuring rather than proof of hypocrisy, asks whether the clay shall contend with the potter, gets a sense of the angels' verse by repeating the negation, and has death still working in us like a mole digging our grave at each remove.

Clarke renders the question as whether sinful man can be justified before God, protests against inferring that no man can be justified at all, prefers the Latin's how much more to the familiar how much less, and turns the phrase about dying without wisdom on his own age's ignorance; Wesley agrees that the angels charged with folly are the fallen ones.

Ellicott calls the question the friends' perpetual burden, orthodox and yet inadequate to Job's case, since the dilemma remains of where God's justice is if he punishes the innocent as the guilty; and he holds the verse about the angels to be general, not a reference to any past act.

debates.issue: Whether the angels charged with folly are the fallen angels

positions.view: Clarke insists the verb is charged and not chargeth, so that the folly belongs to those who kept not their first estate and is not laid to those who stand; Wesley agrees.
Ellicott holds the statement general, referring to no act in the past, and would read putteth and chargeth.

debates.issue: What the oracle's question actually asks

positions.view: Gill rejects the comparative sense as too obvious to need a revelation at all.
Clarke renders it as asking whether man can be justified before God, and limits the meaning to the impossibility of self-atonement.

outliers.view: That whether the apparition came from heaven or hell we do not know, since its communication rankles a wound without providing a cure.

themes: shall mortal man be more just than God
his angels he charged with folly
them that dwell in houses of clay
crushed before the moth
they die, even without wisdom
17.pericope_label: Shall mortal man be more just than God: they die, even without wisdom
